PROPERTY SERVICE WORKERS PROTECTION ACT: JANITORIAL EMPLOYER REGISTRATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS PROPERTY SERVICE WORKERS PROTECTION ACT REGISTRATION INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's Property Service Workers Protection Act (Labor Code Part 4.2, Division 2, commencing with Section 1420), which requires every “employer” of a “covered worker” — in practice, a business that employs janitors directly or that engages a janitorial contractor, subcontractor, or franchise to provide janitorial services — to register annually with the Labor Commissioner before conducting that janitorial business, and which conditions that registration on, among other things, a written application and a sexual violence and harassment prevention training attestation. Acme, Inc. is considering engaging Jordan T. Reyes, in connection with the position of Janitor, to perform or to provide janitorial services that this Act may cover.

This corpus separately includes a Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act — Information Sheet, which addresses a different subject: a successor contractor's duty to retain an incumbent janitorial workforce for a transition period after a change in building-service contractors, not this Act's registration requirement. It also separately includes a Security Guard / Proprietary Security Officer Registration (BSIS) — Information Sheet, describing an unrelated licensing scheme for a different occupation, and a Mandatory Sexual Harassment Prevention Training — Information Sheet describing the general Government Code Section 12950.1 training duty that this Act's own training requirement is stated to replace, not supplement, for the employers this Act covers. This document does not determine whether Acme, Inc.'s or Jordan T. Reyes's specific activities meet the statutory definition of “covered worker” or “employer,” whether any exemption applies, or whether a specific registration, application, or training obligation currently applies to any specific person or entity.

“COVERED WORKER” AND “EMPLOYER” DEFINED
The Property Service Workers Protection Act's registration requirement turns on two statutory definitions in Labor Code Section 1420. A “covered worker” is a janitor — a term the statute ties to the federal Service Contract Act Directory of Occupations — and the definition reaches an individual working in that role as an employee, an independent contractor, or a franchisee, not employees alone. Separately, an “employer” is defined broadly enough to include a business that engages janitorial services by contract, subcontract, or franchise agreement, and not only a business that itself employs janitors directly; the definition specifically excludes the entity that receives the janitorial services from another business under such an arrangement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "“Covered worker” means a janitor, including any individual predominantly working, whether as an employee, independent contractor, or franchisee, as a janitor, as that term is defined in the Service Contract Act Directory of Occupations maintained by the United States Department of Labor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1420(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, definition of “covered worker” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1420.)
  "“Employer” means any person or entity that employs at least one covered worker or otherwise engages by contract, subcontract, or franchise agreement for the provision of janitorial services by one or more covered workers. The term “employer” includes the term “covered successor employer,” but does not include an entity that is the recipient of the janitorial services."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1420(g)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, definition of “employer” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1420.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only subdivisions (b)(1) and (g)(1) of Section 1420, which is a longer definitional section; it does not restate subdivision (b)(2)'s exclusion of workers whose duties are predominantly final construction-related cleanup, subdivision (g)(2)'s separate definition of “covered successor employer,” or the section's remaining definitions of “commissioner,” “current and valid registration,” “department,” “director,” “division,” “production rates,” “shift,” “square footage,” and “supervisor.” This document does not determine whether any specific individual or entity meets either definition.

ANNUAL REGISTRATION WITH THE LABOR COMMISSIONER, EFFECTIVE JULY 1, 2018
Since July 1, 2018, Labor Code Section 1423 has required every employer within the meaning of this Act to register with the Labor Commissioner on an annual basis.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Effective July 1, 2018, every employer shall register with the commissioner annually."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1423 (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, annual registration requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1423.)
  Known gap: Section 1423 states the annual registration duty itself; it does not, in its own text, state the registration fee (addressed in Labor Code Section 1427, in a separate clause of this document), the form the registration takes (addressed in Labor Code Section 1425, not quoted in this document), or the renewal-notice procedure (addressed in Labor Code Section 1426, not quoted in this document). This document does not determine whether any specific person or entity is currently registered.

PROHIBITION ON CONDUCTING JANITORIAL BUSINESS WITHOUT REGISTRATION
Labor Code Section 1428 bars an employer from conducting any janitorial business without complying with this Act's registration requirements, and separately authorizes the commissioner to revoke a registration on a finding that the employer is out of compliance with any requirement of the Act or has failed to satisfy any condition of Section 1429.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "An employer shall not conduct any janitorial business without complying with the registration requirements of this part. The commissioner may revoke a registration if the commissioner finds an employer to be out of compliance with any requirement of this part or to have failed to satisfy any of the conditions of Section 1429."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1428 (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, prohibition on conducting janitorial business without registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1428.)
  Known gap: Section 1428's own text does not itself describe the procedural steps — notice, hearing, or appeal rights — that precede a revocation; that procedure, if any, is not addressed in this document. This document does not determine that any specific employer's conduct has or has not complied with the Act's registration requirements.

REGISTRATION FEE: $500 INITIAL APPLICATION AND $500 ANNUAL RENEWAL
Labor Code Section 1427 sets the registration fee the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement collects from each employer: an initial nonrefundable application fee of $500, and a further annual fee of $500 due on the anniversary of the initial application, with the statute separately permitting the division to periodically adjust the amount to fund the direct and indirect costs of administering and enforcing the Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement shall collect from each employer an initial nonrefundable application fee of five hundred dollars ($500), and an annual fee of five hundred dollars ($500) on the anniversary date of initial application, and may periodically adjust the registration fee in an amount sufficient to fund all direct and indirect costs to administer and enforce this part."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1427 (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, registration fee (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1427.)
  Known gap: Section 1427 authorizes a periodic adjustment of the fee without stating, in its own text, a current adjusted amount if one is now in effect; this document reports only the $500 figures stated directly in the statute's text and does not represent that $500 is necessarily the fee currently being collected.

WRITTEN APPLICATION REQUIREMENT AND THE SEXUAL VIOLENCE AND HARASSMENT PREVENTION TRAINING ATTESTATION
Before approving any employer's registration, Labor Code Section 1429 requires a written application, subscribed and sworn to by the employer. Among the items that application must contain, effective January 1, 2020, is a written attestation to the commissioner that the sexual violence and harassment prevention training the Act separately requires has been provided as required, and effective January 1, 2022, the attestation must also state whether that training was provided by a peer trainer and, if not, why not.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement shall not approve the registration of any employer until all of the following conditions are satisfied:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1429 (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, conditions for approving registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1429.)
  "The employer has executed a written application, in a form prescribed by the commissioner and subscribed and sworn to by the employer, containing all of the following:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1429(a) (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, written application requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1429.)
  "Effective January 1, 2020, all new applications for registration and renewal of registration shall demonstrate completion of the sexual violence and harassment prevention training requirements prescribed by the division and developed pursuant to Section 1429.5 by providing written attestation to the commissioner that the training has been provided as required. Effective January 1, 2022, the attestation shall include whether the training was provided by a peer trainer and an explanation as to why a peer trainer was not used if a peer trainer did not provide the required training."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1429(a)(10) (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, sexual violence and harassment prevention training attestation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1429.)
  Known gap: Section 1429(a) lists eleven separate categories of information a registration application must contain; this clause quotes the section's introductory sentence, subdivision (a)'s own introductory sentence, and paragraph (a)(10)'s training-attestation requirement specifically, and does not restate the other ten categories — among them business-entity details, workers' compensation coverage information, and disclosures about unpaid wages, taxes, and prior citations — or subdivision (b)'s separate fee-payment condition and subdivision (c)'s statement that a violation of the section is not a crime. This document does not determine that any specific employer's application does or does not satisfy these conditions.

BIENNIAL IN-PERSON SEXUAL VIOLENCE AND HARASSMENT PREVENTION TRAINING
Labor Code Section 1429.5(a) required the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement to establish, by January 1, 2019, a biennial in-person sexual violence and harassment prevention training requirement that employers governed by this Act must provide to nonsupervisory covered workers and to supervisors of nonsupervisory covered workers.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement shall establish by January 1, 2019, a biennial in-person sexual violence and harassment prevention training requirement to be provided by employers governed by this part for nonsupervisory covered workers and supervisors of nonsupervisory covered workers."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1429.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, biennial sexual violence and harassment prevention training requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1429.5.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the establishment duty in the first sentence of subdivision (a); it does not restate that subdivision's cross-references to the training-content and trainer-qualification standards of Government Code Section 12950.1, which is addressed in a separate clause of this document, or subdivisions (b) through (k)'s provisions on the training advisory committee, the list of qualified peer-training organizations, per-participant payment rates, and compliance documentation. This document does not determine whether any specific employer has provided this training as required.

THIS ACT'S TRAINING REQUIREMENT REPLACES, RATHER THAN ADDS TO, THE GENERAL FEHA TRAINING DUTY
Section 1429.5(a) states that the training it requires is in lieu of, and not in addition to, the training otherwise required under Government Code Section 12950.1 — the statute this corpus's own Mandatory Sexual Harassment Prevention Training information sheet addresses — provided that the training given under Section 1429.5 meets or exceeds Section 12950.1's own requirements, apart from the separate trainer-qualification rules Section 1429.5 sets for training given to nonsupervisors.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The training required under this section shall be in lieu of, and not in addition to, the requirements for training under Section 12950.1 of the Government Code, as long as the training pursuant to this section meets or exceeds the requirements for training under Section 12950.1 of the Government Code, apart from the aforementioned distinction regarding trainer qualification for nonsupervisory training."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1429.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, training required in lieu of Government Code Section 12950.1 training (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1429.5.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the same subdivision, Section 1429.5(a), as the preceding clause of this document; both clauses draw on the same subdivision rather than on independent sources, which is disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroboration. This document does not determine, for a specific employer, whether training actually provided meets or falls short of Section 12950.1's requirements.

GROUNDS ON WHICH REGISTRATION OR RENEWAL MUST BE DENIED
Labor Code Section 1430 bars the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement from registering or renewing the registration of an employer under specified circumstances, including where the employer has not fully satisfied a final judgment for unpaid wages owed to an employee or former employee of a business the employer is required to register under this Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement shall not register or renew the registration of an employer in any of the following circumstances:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1430 (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, grounds for denying registration or renewal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1430.)
  "The employer has not fully satisfied any final judgment for unpaid wages due to an employee or former employee of a business for which the employer is required to register under this chapter."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1430(a) (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, unsatisfied unpaid-wage judgment as a ground for denial (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1430.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the section's introductory sentence and subdivision (a); it does not restate subdivisions (b) through (e), which separately bar registration or renewal for an unremedied delinquency in Unemployment Insurance Code contributions, an unremedied delinquency in FICA Social Security and Medicare tax contributions, an unsatisfied administrative settlement or final judgment for a Government Code Section 12940 (Fair Employment and Housing Act) violation, or an unsatisfied final judgment for failing to secure valid workers' compensation coverage under Section 3700. This document does not determine that any specific employer does or does not meet any of these grounds.

CIVIL FINES FOR AN UNREGISTERED EMPLOYER AND FOR A PARTY THAT CONTRACTS WITH ONE
Labor Code Section 1432 authorizes a civil fine of $100 for each calendar day an employer required to register under Section 1423 remains unregistered, capped at $10,000. Separately, and directly relevant to a business deciding whether to engage a janitorial contractor rather than employ janitors itself, the same section subjects any person or entity that contracts with an employer lacking a current and valid registration — as shown on the online registration database at the time the contract is executed, extended, renewed, or modified — to a civil fine of between $2,000 and $10,000 for a first violation, and between $10,000 and $25,000 for a subsequent violation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "An employer who fails to register pursuant to Section 1423 is subject to a civil fine of one hundred dollars ($100) for each calendar day that the employer is unregistered, not to exceed ten thousand dollars ($10,000)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1432(a) (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, civil fine for an unregistered employer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1432.)
  "Any person or entity that contracts with an employer who lacks a current and valid registration, as displayed on the online registration database at the time the contract is executed, extended, renewed, or modified, under this part on the date the person or entity enters into or renews a contract or subcontract for janitorial services with the employer is subject to a civil fine of not less than two thousand dollars ($2,000) nor more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) in the case of a first violation, and a civil fine of not less than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) nor more than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000) for a subsequent violation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1432(b) (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, civil fine for a party that contracts with an unregistered janitorial employer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1432.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only subdivisions (a) and (b) of Section 1432; it does not restate subdivision (c)'s separate $10,000-per-violation fine for a material misrepresentation in a registration application, or subdivision (d)'s statement that enforcement authority rests exclusively with the commissioner under the procedures set out in Section 1197.1. This document does not calculate any specific fine amount and does not determine that any specific employer or contracting party is subject to a fine.

PUBLIC DATABASE OF REGISTERED PROPERTY SERVICE EMPLOYERS
Labor Code Section 1431 requires the commissioner to maintain a public database, on the department's website, of property service employers — listing each registrant's name, address, and registration number, whether the registrant is a nonemployee registrant exempt from the workers' compensation coverage requirement of Section 3700, and the registration's effective dates. This is the same online database Section 1432(b) refers to as the reference point for whether a janitorial contractor's registration was current when a contracting party executed, extended, renewed, or modified a contract with it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The commissioner shall maintain a public database of property service employers, on the internet website of the department, including the name, address, registration number, whether the registrant is a nonemployee registrant exempt from the requirement to secure workers’ compensation coverage under Section 3700 of the Labor Code, and effective dates of registration."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1431 (California Legislative Information text), Property Service Workers Protection Act, public database of registered employers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1431.)
  Known gap: A CourtListener case-law search conducted for this document, for published opinions construing the Act's registration or training provisions, returned no on-point results; this document proceeds on the statutory text alone and does not represent that no such case law exists, only that this search did not surface any to cite. This document does not determine that any specific employer's entry in the database, or absence from it, is current or accurate as of any particular date.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet regarding the Property Service Workers Protection Act's registration requirement was reviewed by Acme, Inc. in connection with Jordan T. Reyes's prospective position of Janitor on September 9, 2026. It reflects the statutory text as of the date checked in each authority section above and does not reflect any amendments made after that date, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.

Reviewed by (on behalf of Acme, Inc.): ______________________
Date: September 9, 2026

citations.quote: An employer who fails to register pursuant to Section 1423 is subject to a civil fine of one hundred dollars ($100) for each calendar day that the employer is unregistered, not to exceed ten thousand dollars ($10,000).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1432(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Property Service Workers Protection Act, civil fine for a party that contracts with an unregistered janitorial employer
citations.quote: Any person or entity that contracts with an employer who lacks a current and valid registration, as displayed on the online registration database at the time the contract is executed, extended, renewed, or modified, under this part on the date the person or entity enters into or renews a contract or subcontract for janitorial services with the employer is subject to a civil fine of not less than two thousand dollars ($2,000) nor more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) in the case of a first violation, and a civil fine of not less than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) nor more than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000) for a subsequent violation.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes only subdivisions (a) and (b) of Section 1432; it does not restate subdivision (c)'s separate $10,000-per-violation fine for a material misrepresentation in a registration application, or subdivision (d)'s statement that enforcement authority rests exclusively with the commissioner under the procedures set out in Section 1197.1. This document does not calculate any specific fine amount and does not determine that any specific employer or contracting party is subject to a fine.

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code Section 1431 requires the commissioner to maintain a public database, on the department's website, of property service employers — listing each registrant's name, address, and registration number, whether the registrant is a nonemployee registrant exempt from the workers' compensation coverage requirement of Section 3700, and the registration's effective dates. This is the same online database Section 1432(b) refers to as the reference point for whether a janitorial contractor's registration was current when a contracting party executed, extended, renewed, or modified a contract with it.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1431 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Property Service Workers Protection Act, public database of registered employers
citations.quote: The commissioner shall maintain a public database of property service employers, on the internet website of the department, including the name, address, registration number, whether the registrant is a nonemployee registrant exempt from the requirement to secure workers’ compensation coverage under Section 3700 of the Labor Code, and effective dates of registration.

expectedJSON.gap: A CourtListener case-law search conducted for this document, for published opinions construing the Act's registration or training provisions, returned no on-point results; this document proceeds on the statutory text alone and does not represent that no such case law exists, only that this search did not surface any to cite. This document does not determine that any specific employer's entry in the database, or absence from it, is current or accurate as of any particular date.
